h1: Arizona HOA Special Assessment Challenge Letter Generator
metaTitle: Arizona HOA Special Assessment Challenge Letter | $19
metaDescription: Challenge an Arizona HOA special assessment. Generate a demand letter that cites A.R.S. § 33-1805 and requests the records behind it. $19.
deadline: 10 business days for the HOA to make records available for examination or provide copies (A.R.S. § 33-1805)

introParagraph: If your Arizona HOA hit you with a sudden special assessment, you have real legal options. Arizona law limits how a homeowners association can raise assessments, and many boards skip steps their own documents require, such as proper notice or a member vote. Whether you live in a planned community governed by A.R.S. § 33-1803 or a condominium under A.R.S. § 33-1255, these statutes require open meetings, access to records, and adherence to your CC&Rs. A well-drafted challenge letter citing Arizona-specific statutes often resolves the dispute without litigation. This tool generates a customized demand letter referencing the exact Arizona laws your HOA must follow, demanding documentation, and preserving your rights before the assessment lien attaches to your property.
lawExplanation: Arizona regulates HOA special assessments through two primary statutes. For planned communities, A.R.S. § 33-1803(A) provides that an association may not impose a regular assessment more than 20% greater than the prior fiscal year's assessment without the approval of a majority of the members, unless the community documents set a lower limit. For condominiums, A.R.S. § 33-1255 requires assessments to be made at least annually, based on a budget the association adopts at least annually. Both statutes require the HOA to follow the procedures laid out in its own declaration (CC&Rs) and bylaws. If those documents require a member vote, notice period, or quorum for special assessments, the board cannot bypass those rules. A.R.S. § 33-1804 mandates open meetings, meaning special assessment decisions generally must occur at a properly noticed open board meeting where members can attend and speak. A.R.S. § 33-1805 makes the association's financial and other records reasonably available for examination, with ten business days to fulfill a request, subject to listed exceptions such as privileged attorney communications and pending litigation — critical evidence when challenging an assessment. If the HOA fails to follow statutory or governing-document procedures, the assessment can be challenged as unenforceable. Homeowners may also dispute assessments imposed for purposes outside the HOA's authority, such as luxury upgrades not authorized by the declaration. Importantly, A.R.S. § 33-1807 governs assessment liens: foreclosure is allowed only if the owner has been delinquent for eighteen months or in the amount of $10,000 or more (for a special assessment of $10,000 or more, only the eighteen-month threshold applies), and the board must make reasonable efforts to offer a payment plan before filing. Under A.R.S. § 32-2199.01, homeowners may also file a petition with the Arizona Department of Real Estate's Office of Administrative Hearings to challenge HOA violations of statute or governing documents, an alternative to court that requires a filing fee set by the Department.
letterStrategy: A strong Arizona HOA special assessment challenge letter accomplishes several goals at once. First, it formally disputes the assessment in writing, which preserves your rights and stops the HOA from claiming you waived objections by paying without protest. Second, it demands specific documentation under A.R.S. § 33-1805, including the meeting minutes approving the assessment, the notice sent to members, the budget or reserve study justifying the amount, any vote tally, and the section of the CC&Rs authorizing the charge. The HOA has 10 business days to comply. Third, the letter cites the exact statutes the HOA appears to have violated — whether that is the open meeting requirement under A.R.S. § 33-1804, the budget ratification process, or a CC&R provision requiring member approval. Finally, it warns of escalation: an administrative petition with the Arizona Department of Real Estate, a small claims or superior court action, and, if the dispute reaches court, a request for costs and attorney fees where the law allows. Boards know that fighting a meritorious challenge can cost the association far more than rescinding the assessment. Most disputes resolve at the letter stage because management companies recognize procedural defects and recommend the board cure them.
proceduralNotes: The small claims division of Arizona Justice Court handles claims up to $5,000 (A.R.S. § 22-503), and Justice Court has jurisdiction over civil actions up to $10,000 (A.R.S. § 22-201); larger amounts go to Superior Court. Alternatively, A.R.S. § 32-2199.01 allows an owner to petition the Arizona Department of Real Estate for a hearing on violations of the planned community statutes or documents, with a filing fee set by the Department; if the petitioner prevails, the administrative law judge must order the respondent to pay the petitioner the filing fee (A.R.S. § 32-2199.02). An action for debt founded on a written contract executed in Arizona must be brought within six years (A.R.S. § 12-548), but act quickly — once an HOA records a lien, removal becomes harder. In a lien action under A.R.S. § 33-1807, the judgment may include costs and reasonable attorney fees for the prevailing party, which applies to both sides.

faq.q: Can my Arizona HOA impose a special assessment without a vote?
faq.a: It depends on your CC&Rs. Some declarations allow the board to levy special assessments unilaterally up to a certain dollar amount or percentage, while others require a member vote. Under A.R.S. § 33-1803(A), a regular assessment more than 20% above the prior year's generally requires approval of a majority of the members, and the community documents may set a lower limit but not a higher one. Special assessments are governed mainly by your declaration. Always read your governing documents carefully — if the board skipped a required vote or notice, the assessment may be unenforceable.

faq.q: What records can I demand from my HOA?
faq.a: Under A.R.S. § 33-1805 (planned communities) and A.R.S. § 33-1258 (condominiums), Arizona homeowners have the right to examine the association's financial and other records, which must be made reasonably available. The association has ten business days to fulfill a request to examine or to provide copies, may not charge for making records available for review, and may charge up to fifteen cents per page for copies. Some records may be withheld, such as privileged attorney communications and records relating to pending litigation.

faq.q: What if I just refuse to pay the special assessment?
faq.a: Refusing to pay is risky. The HOA has a lien for the assessment from the time it becomes due, and under A.R.S. § 33-1807 it may foreclose only after the owner has been delinquent for eighteen months or in the amount of $10,000 or more, after reasonable efforts to offer a payment plan. The better path is to pay under written protest while formally challenging the assessment, or to file an administrative petition with the Arizona Department of Real Estate before the lien attaches. A demand letter often resolves the dispute before payment is due. Consult an attorney before withholding payment on a contested assessment.

faq.q: Can I file a complaint with the Arizona Department of Real Estate?
faq.a: Yes. Under A.R.S. § 32-2199.01, Arizona homeowners can file a petition with the Department of Real Estate alleging the HOA violated state statute or its own governing documents. The matter is heard by an Office of Administrative Hearings judge. The petition requires a filing fee set by the Department; if you prevail, the judge must order the respondent to pay you the filing fee. This is often faster and cheaper than court and is a valuable option for special assessment challenges based on procedural violations.

faq.q: Will I get my attorney fees back if I win?
faq.a: Possibly. In a lien action under A.R.S. § 33-1807, the judgment may include costs and reasonable attorney fees for the prevailing party, and a court may award fees to the successful party in a contested action arising out of a contract (A.R.S. § 12-341.01). This cuts both ways — if the HOA wins, you could owe their fees. That risk is exactly why a well-documented demand letter citing specific statutory violations is so effective: it shows the board that defending a weak assessment could be more expensive than rescinding it.
